The Week Pitch Day Learnings Thank You
MBA Capstone · August 2026

What I learned beyond
the business case

A personal reflection on Capstone Week in London: leading a cross-industry team, pitching for real judges, and the lessons I'm bringing back into my work at Laerdal.

Author Yuanzhen Cai · Laerdal Medical Result 🥈 Second Place + Distinction Published September 2026

Getting to use Laerdal's Sim to Improve initiative as our capstone project was something I felt genuinely grateful for. It's an innovative and meaningful idea, one that addresses a real gap in how hospitals improve care quality, and that meaning came through. My teammates felt it. The professors felt it. That shared sense of purpose made a real difference to how we showed up during the week.

I recruited five teammates from across the healthcare industry: medical devices, pharma, and healthcare operations. All directors and senior managers with deep domain expertise. Getting that group together was one of the better decisions of the process. Getting them to work well together was the harder part.

Capstone Week · 16–22 August 2026

One very intense week on campus

The structure was consistent: morning lectures with a different professor each day, followed by afternoon coaching sessions and team work sessions. Six days of that, with Pitch Day at the end.

Each day brought a different lens on the business case, with a different professor asking hard questions about our assumptions.

The topics we covered across the week:

Entrepreneurial Opportunities Customer Insights & Opportunity Prioritisation Business Models & Platform Economics Performing Business Experiments Resource Mobilisation How to Pitch

Coaching every afternoon

Each afternoon, a professor would coach us through the business case. That meant pitching and defending to a new expert every single day. Some of them didn't immediately understand what Sim to Improve was, which turned out to be valuable: it forced us to simplify, find better analogies, and lead with the problem rather than the product.

We rewrote parts of the pitch multiple times across the week. By Pitch Day, the opening story had become the strongest part of the deck.
Pitch Day · 22 August

The judges, the pitch, and a very close finish

The final pitch was judged by Bruce Hellman and Mariam Makhmutova, both with healthcare backgrounds, exactly the audience we had prepared for.

We opened with Mia's story: a patient who becomes the first test of an untested clinical system. That framing landed. The judges said it clearly at the end: the case was compelling, the storytelling was strong, and the commercial opportunity was clear.

🥈
Second Place: the judges said it was very close
We pitched against projects from Philips and Siemens, among others. The professors said they would love to hear how this project develops. Not a standard comment.
Beyond the Classroom

Building a cohort, not just a team

The capstone week wasn't only about the pitch. Our whole cohort spent evenings together: an escape room, a group dinner, and those moments mattered. A group of people from very different industries, pushed through the same intensity, building something real between them.

Outcome

Distinction, and work that's already in use

After Pitch Day, we had one more week to complete the extended business case deck. The course result: a Distinction.

Several team members posted on LinkedIn thanking Laerdal for the opportunity and the project. Unprompted. It shows the work meant something beyond the grade.

Back in Stavanger, I shared the capstone findings with the Sim to Improve business team. Their feedback: the storytelling approach and the commercial visualisations were especially useful, content they could directly bring into their own stakeholder conversations. That felt like the right outcome: not an academic exercise, but something with real practical value.

What I'm Taking Away

Three lessons I'll carry into my work

Lesson 01

Team building is more than matching expertise

I recruited for background and domain knowledge, and found five highly capable people. What I didn't account for was personality and working style. One team member was very assertive in a way that created friction I hadn't anticipated and didn't have good tools to navigate at the time.

I also didn't speak to people who'd worked with them before. In a high-pressure, short-timeline team, character matters as much as competence. Going forward: when building a team for anything critical, I'll assess for both, and ask around first.

Next time: interview for personality, not just experience
Lesson 02

Storytelling is a core business skill, not a soft one

My design background naturally drew me toward storytelling and visualisation. Part of me wished I'd been more involved in the financial modelling and business architecture, areas I felt less confident in.

But the coaching sessions were a reality check: storytelling was the area where we were weakest, and improving it is what moved our pitch up significantly. Getting buy-in from investors, clinicians, or internal leadership requires the ability to make complex ideas feel obvious. That's not decoration; it's strategy. I'm reframing it as a genuine strength to develop deliberately.

Insight: narrative clarity is what turns ideas into decisions
Lesson 03

A business case needs a point of view, not just analysis

One thing the coaching sessions surfaced repeatedly: the difference between a slide that presents options and a slide that argues a position. We had a lot of the former early in the week. The professors kept pushing us to make a choice, commit to a recommendation, and then defend it.

That shift, from analyst to advocate, is something I want to bring back into my UX and product work too. Research and analysis are inputs. A clear, defensible point of view is the output that actually moves things forward.

Insight: take a position, don't just map the landscape
